[Francis Olympic Field](/wiki/Francis_Olympic_Field "Francis Olympic Field") of [Washington University in St. Louis](/wiki/Washington_University_in_St._Louis "Washington University in St. Louis"), site of the [1904 Olympic Games](/wiki/1904_Summer_Olympics "1904 Summer Olympics"). The 1904 Summer Olympics in St. Louis, Missouri were the first Olympic Games held outside of Europe.

The United States made its Olympic debut in 1896 in [Athens](/wiki/Athens "Athens"), the very first [edition](/wiki/1896_Summer_Olympics "1896 Summer Olympics") of the modern games. The nation performed inconsistently in the pre-[World War-I](/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") period, primarily due to fielding considerably fewer athletes than host countries, with the exception being the [1904 Olympics](/wiki/1904_Summer_Olympics "1904 Summer Olympics") in [St. Louis](/wiki/St._Louis "St. Louis"), [Missouri](/wiki/Missouri "Missouri"), where the U.S. achieved its largest medal haul in history, a record that still stands today. During the [interwar period](/wiki/Interwar_period "Interwar period"), the U.S. enjoyed its greatest success, topping both gold and total medal counts at four straight Summer Games, before falling short in the [1936 Berlin games](/wiki/1936_Summer_Olympics "1936 Summer Olympics"). The next summer Olympics were held in [1948](/wiki/1948_Summer_Olympics "1948 Summer Olympics") following [World War II](/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). In [1952](/wiki/1952_Summer_Olympics "1952 Summer Olympics"), the [Soviet Union](/wiki/Soviet_Union_at_the_Olympics "Soviet Union at the Olympics") made its Olympic debut, initiating a state-sponsored approach to international sport focused on projecting socio-political superiority. University of Rostock :: History :: 1419–1919 :: chunk_0001
The university was founded in 1419 by confirmation of [Pope Martin V](/wiki/Pope_Martin_V "Pope Martin V") and thus is one of the oldest universities in Northern Europe.

In Germany, there are only five universities that were founded earlier, while only Heidelberg and Leipzig operated continuously since then: [Heidelberg](/wiki/University_of_Heidelberg "University of Heidelberg") (1386), [Cologne](/wiki/University_of_Cologne "University of Cologne") (1388/1919), [Erfurt](/wiki/University_of_Erfurt "University of Erfurt") (1392/1994), [Würzburg](/wiki/University_of_W%C3%BCrzburg "University of Würzburg") (1402/1582) and [Leipzig](/wiki/University_of_Leipzig "University of Leipzig") (1409).
That makes Rostock University the third oldest German university in continuous operation.

Throughout the 15th and 16th centuries, the University of Rostock had about 400 to 500 students each year and was among the most important universities in Germany and Northern Europe at the time, with many of its students originating from the [Low Countries](/wiki/Low_Countries "Low Countries"), [Scandinavia](/wiki/Scandinavia "Scandinavia") or other countries bordering the [Baltic Sea](/wiki/Baltic_Sea "Baltic Sea").

In the course of political struggles and due to pressure from the church, the university moved to [Greifswald](/wiki/Greifswald "Greifswald") in 1437 and remained there until 1443. From 1487 to 1488 teaching took place in [Lübeck](/wiki/L%C3%BCbeck "Lübeck"). A few years after the city of Rostock, the university became [Protestant](/wiki/Protestant "Protestant") in 1542. Henceforth, [Humanism](/wiki/Humanism "Humanism") and [Lutheranism](/wiki/Lutheranism "Lutheranism") were defining characteristics of the university.

In the 16th century, Rostock was the first university to teach [Copernicanism](/wiki/Copernicanism "Copernicanism"), which was introduced by Professor [Duncan Liddel](/wiki/Duncan_Liddel "Duncan Liddel").[[10]](#cite_note-10) After the [Thirty Years' War](/wiki/Thirty_Years%27_War "Thirty Years' War") (1618–1648), however, for about two centuries the University of Rostock played only a regional role.

A human Moon landing posed several daunting technical challenges to the US and USSR. Besides guidance and weight management, [atmospheric re-entry](/wiki/Atmospheric_re-entry "Atmospheric re-entry") without [ablative](/wiki/Ablation "Ablation") overheating was a major hurdle. After the Soviets launched [Sputnik](/wiki/Sputnik "Sputnik"), von Braun promoted a plan for the US Army to establish a military lunar outpost by 1965.

Rodin was born in [Philadelphia, Pennsylvania](/wiki/Philadelphia,_Pennsylvania "Philadelphia, Pennsylvania"),[[4]](#cite_note-4) on September 9, 1944, as Judith Seitz. She grew up in a middle-class [Jewish](/wiki/Jewish "Jewish") family and was the younger of two daughters of Morris and Sally Seitz.[[5]](#cite_note-Jspace-list-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6) She graduated with honors from the [Philadelphia High School for Girls](/wiki/Philadelphia_High_School_for_Girls "Philadelphia High School for Girls") and won an undergraduate scholarship to the University of Pennsylvania.[[7]](#cite_note-NYTProfile-7)

At Penn, Rodin majored in [psychology](/wiki/Psychology "Psychology") and graduated from the university's College for Women with a B.A. in 1966. She was the president of Penn's Women's Student Government and led the groundwork for the merger with the Men's Student Government[[8]](#cite_note-8) that ultimately formed the Student Committee on Undergraduate Education (SCUE) in 1965 that led to the co-education of the College of Arts and Sciences.[[9]](#cite_note-9) She went on to earn a Ph.D. from [Columbia University](/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University"), which she received in 1970. Rodin completed postdoctoral research at the [University of California at Irvine](/wiki/University_of_California_at_Irvine "University of California at Irvine") in 1971.[[10]](#cite_note-RockCV-10)

Relief map of Belgium

Belgium shares borders with [France](/wiki/France "France") (620 km; 390 mi), [Germany](/wiki/Germany "Germany") (162/167 km), [Luxembourg](/wiki/Luxembourg "Luxembourg") (148 km; 92 mi), and the [Netherlands](/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands") (450 km; 280 mi). Its total surface, including water area, is 30,689 km2 (11,849 sq mi).[[5]](#cite_note-area-5) Before 2018, its total area was believed to be 30,528 km2 (11,787 sq mi). However, when the country's statistics were measured in 2018, a new calculation method was used. Unlike previous calculations, this one included the area from the coast to the low-water line, revealing the country to be 160 km2 (62 sq mi) larger in surface area than previously thought.[[50]](#cite_note-statbel-61)[[51]](#cite_note-hetlaatste-62) Its land area alone is 30,494 km2 (11,774 sq mi).[[6]](#cite_note-land-6) It lies between latitudes 49°30' and 51°30' N, and longitudes 2°33' and 6°24' E.[[52]](#cite_note-nCHdl-63)

Belgium has three main geographical regions; the coastal plain in the northwest and the central plateau both belong to the Anglo-Belgian Basin, and the [Ardennes](/wiki/Ardennes "Ardennes") uplands in the southeast to the [Hercynian orogenic belt](/wiki/Variscan_orogeny "Variscan orogeny"). The [Paris Basin](/wiki/Paris_Basin "Paris Basin") reaches a small fourth area at Belgium's southernmost tip, [Belgian Lorraine](/wiki/Belgian_Lorraine "Belgian Lorraine").[[53]](#cite_note-KKuI7-64)

The coastal plain consists mainly of sand dunes and [polders](/wiki/Polder "Polder").
